analysis.subject: chemistry
analysis.pageCoverage: Page covers plutonium creation in reactors, radiation types and toxicity, common isotopes and half-lives, transformation to daughter products, uses in pacemakers and space missions, and reprocessing of spent fuel into mixed oxide fuel.

overview.headline: Plutonium isotopes, half-lives, decay and reactor fuel cycle

keyPoints.point: Plutonium is a radioactive metallic element produced in reactors when uranium absorbs neutrons
keyPoints.quote: Plutonium is a radioactive metallic element with the atomic number 94.

keyPoints.point: Plutonium emits alpha particles that are easily stopped with short range and can be toxic if inhaled
keyPoints.quote: Plutonium predominantly emits alpha particles – a type of radiation that is easily stopped and has a short range.

keyPoints.point: Different plutonium isotopes have different half-lives and shorter half-lives decay more quickly with more energetic radioactivity
keyPoints.quote: Substances with shorter half-lives decay more quickly than those with longer half-lives, so they emit more energetic radioactivity.

keyPoints.point: Spent fuel contains plutonium that can be separated by reprocessing to produce mixed oxide fuel for power reactors
keyPoints.quote: Spent nuclear fuel from U.S. reactors contains about 1 percent plutonium by weight.

keyTerms.gloss: radioactive metallic element created in reactors when uranium absorbs neutrons
keyTerms.quote: Plutonium is a radioactive metallic element with the atomic number 94.

keyTerms.gloss: different forms of plutonium with different half-lives such as common plutonium types
keyTerms.quote: There are five “common” isotopes of plutonium, Pu-238, Pu-239, Pu-240, Pu-241, and Pu-242.

keyTerms.gloss: interval measured in years for plutonium to lose half its radioactivity
keyTerms.quote: Pu-239 has a half-life of 24,100 years and Pu-241’s half-life is 14.4 years.

keyTerms.gloss: nucleus can easily split apart when struck by a neutron
keyTerms.quote: These are all “fissionable” – the atom’s nucleus can easily split apart if it is struck by a neutron.

keyTerms.gloss: uses chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium and other fission products
keyTerms.quote: This process, known as reprocessing, uses chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium and other fission products.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Teaches half-life definition and provides isotope half-lives for interactive decay modeling
componentPlan.focusQuote: The different isotopes have different “half-lives” – the time it takes to lose half of its radioactivity.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Supports recall of checkable facts about plutonium uses and spent fuel composition
componentPlan.focusQuote: Spent nuclear fuel from U.S. reactors contains about 1 percent plutonium by weight.
